title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Two studies appear to disagree about AI adoption in employee relations. What does their difference actually measure? `[V]`
options: One surveyed larger organizations than the other

One asked organizations where AI is deployed across HR practice areas — institutional adoption — while the other asked ER teams what they had done, where "experimented with" is a low bar; the gap between them is unsanctioned use
One measured intent and the other measured spending
They used incompatible definitions of artificial intelligence
questions.explanation: Both are sound. The organizational answer to "have we deployed AI in employee relations" is no, and it is wrong — which is the diagnosis: the function has adopted AI without adopting it.

questions.prompt: Why does the module say a prohibition produces concealment rather than compliance?
options: Because employees resent restrictions on tools they find useful
Because the workload makes compliance impossible, so you end up with the same exposure plus no record of it and no way to know which case files were affected
Because prohibitions are unenforceable without monitoring software
Because AI use is difficult to detect in written work product
questions.explanation: Which is why the audit has to be framed without penalty: you are not trying to find out whether somebody broke a rule, you are trying to find out which files are affected, and only one framing returns that.

questions.prompt: What are the five rungs of the evidentiary ladder, in order?
options: Intake, investigation, analysis, decision, appeal
Allegation, evidence, interview, report, outcome
Observation, corroboration, inference, finding, determination
Fact, context, judgment, conclusion, sanction
questions.explanation: It is how investigators are already trained to write, which is why it is a working instrument rather than a diagram — and AI's permission changes at every rung.

questions.prompt: Where does AI's permission stop on the ladder?
options: After observation — anything interpretive is off limits
After inference, and only for generating untested possibilities; nothing at finding or determination
After corroboration
At determination only, since findings are factual rather than evaluative
questions.explanation: At rung three it may generate candidate possibilities you then test — never rank them, never select one. Rungs four and five are the boundary, because both require weighing.

questions.prompt: Why is "AI may help with summaries" described as an unusable rule?
options: Because summaries are not a defined work-product type
Because a summary can sit on any rung, and the same request produces rung-two output or rung-four output depending on how it was phrased
Because summarization is prohibited for confidential material
Because summaries cannot be verified against sources
questions.explanation: Which is why the control is the rung boundary rather than the task: "AI may establish what exists and may not weigh it" is a rule you can apply to a single sentence.

questions.prompt: Which rung does the module identify as the most valuable for AI?
options: Observation, because transcription saves the most time
Corroboration — locating what exists, what conflicts, and what is missing, which is where cases are won and lost
Inference, because generating possibilities is where models are strongest
Finding, with human review
questions.explanation: The missing statement, the document nobody requested, the witness nobody interviewed. The ladder tells you where the leverage is, not only where AI stops.

questions.prompt: Why is intake triage the highest-risk automation target in this function? `[V]`
options: Because intake volumes are the highest of any process

Because it is a determination about whether an allegation is investigated at all, and the person whose complaint was downgraded never appears in your substantiation data — so the failure is structurally unmeasurable
Because intake records are the most likely to be discoverable
Because triage rules change frequently as policy changes
questions.explanation: And worse than the general case elsewhere in this curriculum, because this person had a right to be heard and knows they raised something. Your metrics show a healthy function; their experience is that nothing happened.

questions.prompt: What does the module recommend adding regardless of how you handle triage? `[V]`
options: A second reviewer on every intake decision
Automated keyword flagging for protected-characteristic language
Tracking downgraded and closed-at-intake matters as a category, with a reason and a named decider, and sampling them
A fixed minimum investigation for every complaint received
questions.explanation: Not to second-guess every call — to find out whether the pattern of "no" has a shape. It is the only way the invisible failure becomes visible, and 38% of organizations have no required process that would catch it otherwise.
